messages.subject: split beanplot in ggplot2 - adjusting bandwidth
messages.subject_clean: split beanplot in ggplot2 - adjusting bandwidth
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm attempting to create a split beanplot in ggplot2 and have figured most of it out except how to adjust the bandwidth for the density statistic.  I read early that geom_violin will not plot 2 separate sets of data and that geom_ribbon should be used to create a split beanplot.  So, I was able to create this as a quick example that does a split beanplot of mpg for 6-cylinder vehicles vs 8 cylinder vehicles:

p <- ggplot(mtcars)
p + geom_ribbon(data=subset(mtcars,mtcars$cyl==6),
               aes(x=mpg,ymax=..density..,ymin=0),stat="density") +
           geom_ribbon(data=subset(mtcars,mtcars$cyl==8),
             aes(x=mpg,ymax=0,ymin=-..density..),stat="density")

What I can't figure out is how to adjust the bandwidth (e.g. as with 'adjust' in geom_density) for the density statistic in the ribbon plot to make the density plots either more or less smooth.  Or, is there a better way to go about this than what I've currently tried?

Any advice you might have on this would be greatly appreciated!  Thank you for your help!

cheers,
Andy

messages.subject: Re: Stacked bar plot filled with symbols/lines
messages.subject_clean: Stacked bar plot filled with symbols/lines
messages.body_plain:
The human eye-brain combination tends to focus on areas of contrast (change from one color/shade to another).  When you fill boxes with a solid color (or shade of grey) then the focus is on the boundaries, but when you fill a box with diagonal lines, hash marks, grids, symbols, etc. then the eye is often drawn to the contrast within the box rather than the boundary of the box and this will make it harder for the viewer of the graph to make meaningful comparisons.  This can be a "Fuzzy Box" effect where the size of the box is not interpreted well.  It can even cause a Moire effect where parts of the plot appear to move, even causing motion sickness in some viewers (see the book by Tufte).

The use of the diagonal lines and other patterns date back to the days when the best way to get a color graphic was to use a mechanical pen plotter (a mechanical arm moved a pen around on the paper) and it was impractical to completely fill the area (a high density would do it in theory, but it was really slow (making all the other people waiting to plot something mad) and often tore holes in the paper).  With modern monitors and printers it is better to use solid fills if you are doing a bar chart.

If you are trying to find an alternative to using color (because you need to use a black and white medium, or it may be photocopied, etc.) then consider using a dotplot instead of a barplot, it has a much better data to ink ratio anyways.

If ggplot2 does not have a means to fill barplots with lines/symbols, then that should be considered a feature and evidence of well thought out design rather than any type of lack.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot for your answer,

finally I decided to dodge my stacked bar plot and use a scale of grey colors. I was afraid that on top of each other they might be hard to discern, especially since some categories have low values. Here's a final result:

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-tN83EhS0D5I/Ufq_kAVVprI/AAAAAAAAAJ8/ebPihH3DCig/s1600/C2F6_StackGreyDodge.png>

Here is the script if anyone needs to do something similar :

Plot1 <- ggplot(Data,aes(factor(Model),fill=factor(Data$New.Curve))) +
  geom_bar(position="dodge") +
  labs(x="Model", y="Count") +
  ggtitle(paste("Best models by year for ", File[e], sep="")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=Coul) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size= 18)) +
  theme(legend.background = element_rect(fill="grey95"))+
  theme(legend.key = element_rect(colour = "grey95",fill="grey95"))+
  theme(legend.key.size = unit(1, "cm"))+
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 15))+
  theme(legend.title = element_text(size = 18))+
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 14))+
  theme(legend.margin = unit(1,"cm"))+
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(vjust=-0.5))+
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text( vjust=0, angle=90))+
  theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1,0.2,2,1), "cm"))+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size=19, face="bold", vjust=2.2))+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())+
  labs(fill="Curve")

Plot1

Cheers

JM

messages.subject_clean: Axes on both sides of a graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

It seems there is no way to draw axes on both sides of a graph in ggplot.  I know that Hadley has a distaste about putting two different scales on the same graph, but it seems even drawing the same axes twice is not possible.  Cleveland (1994) advocates for tick marks on both Y axes, both on the left and the right.  (Though the labels typically appear only on one side.)  One reason to put tick marks on both sides is so that a person viewing the graph can see the position on the scale of plot symbols that are on the right side of the data frame as well as they can the position on the scale of plot symbols that are on the left side of the data frame.  The grid lines that ggplot uses sometimes visually interfere with the data plots, so I need to use tick marks instead.

So is there any way around to draw axes on both Y axes?

Thanks,
YZ

References

Cleveland, W. S. (1994). The elements of graphing data (revised ed.). Murray Hill, N.J.: AT&T Bell Laboratories.

>    x = c(rep(1, 3), rep(2, 6), rep(2, 4), rep(3, 2)),

>    geom_raster() +

> ## Theoretically want something like (with some sort of way to specify ranges)
> # + scale_fill_gradient(low = "blue", high = "green")

There is scale_fill_gradientn which allows you to specify multiple
points on the color gradient, not just the ends.

If you are wanting different gradients for different parts of the plot,

> Figure out each gradient range manually and then use scale_fill_manual to stack them up and apply the values there.
> Create multiple plots, where I change the limits and low/high arguments to scale_fill_gradient to basically show each range on its own (with the others greyed out).
> Use the trans argument to transform the scale. I tried that with log but it still didn't look great.
>
> Any suggestions are greatly appreciated.
>
> Best wishes,
> Doug
>

df$out <-""

Which medians do you wish to connect?

Seems to me that you'd have to summarize your data using ddply and then plot the medians on top of the boxplots. Something like this:

require(plyr)

df.med<-ddply(df, .(group), function(x) median(x))

ggplot()+
geom_boxplot(data=df, aes(x = time, y = y, fill = group))+
geom_point(data=df.med, aes(x=time, y=V1, colour=group), position=position_dodge(width=.75))+
geom_line(data=df.med, aes(x=time, y=V1, colour=group, group=group), position=position_dodge(width=.75))

HTH,

B

I don't have a solution to the original problem, but I suspect there simply isn't a knob for that. But I don't think there is a label.hjust bug (other than perhaps a documentation issue; like all the other hjust arguments it should be between zero and 1). label.hjust works as intended:

p+scale_fill_discrete(breaks = levels(PlantGrowth$group),
                      labels = c("short", "longer", "a really long label"),
                      guide = guide_legend(label.hjust=0))

p+scale_fill_discrete(breaks = levels(PlantGrowth$group),
                      labels = c("short", "longer", "a really long label"),
                      guide = guide_legend(label.hjust=1))

​it's just not intended for what you are trying to do with it.

Best,
Ista​

messages.subject_clean: plots with multiple y-axes
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

@hadley and other authors if any: thanks for ggplot and relating packages, I am a new user of them and slowly start to adapt to the gg logic ;)

I would just like to voice an opinion regarding multiple y axes, mainly referring to this discussion:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/3099219/how-to-use-ggplot2-make-plot-with-2-y-axes-one-y-axis-on-the-left-and-another

I write here because that discussion thread is quite old. I hope this is an ok place to put my thoughts.

In the discussion thread, people argue that multiple y axes are "fundamentally flawed", and give good reasons for that. I work in environmental sciences and use them nonetheless, despite the flaws.
I feel I have fairly good reasons, and they relate to measured (and possibly aggregated) time series.

Environmental measurement data often includes multiple variables in inconvertible units. They are however tightly related in a spatial sense. A classic, I would argue, are climate diagrams combining precip and air temp. Another example to highlight the advantage of such plots are time series of river discharge and riverine dissolved ion concentrations. There is usually some form of relationship between both variables, and plotting concentration-discharge relationships is of course a useful analysis approach; but then, there can be a multitude of different signals in there as well, from long-term trends to seasonal signals (think snow cover, soil moisture), and over regular artificial (e.g. fertilisation) to episodic event signals (e.g. point source pollution spikes). All of these can be readily assessed (qualitatively) using time series overlays with independent y axis scaling, and help to characterize such data sets.

I just wanted to put this opinion out somewhere. Maybe this a feature which could be considered for some future release of ggplot2 after all.

Regards, Rene

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one way you can do it. The trick is to make both TREAT and RAND numeric and then adjust some labels at the end. I don't like using qplot() for this type of thing so I'm using the ggplot() approach which affords more control of where to define the aesthetics.
After creating the data frame r from your supplied data set,

library(ggplot2)
r <- read.csv("random.csv", header = TRUE)

# Create numeric versions of TREAT and RAND
r$treat <- as.numeric(r$TREAT)
r$rand <- as.numeric(r$RAND)

# Plot with numeric versions of TREAT and RAND. This makes it easier
# to add text labels later.
p <- ggplot(r) +
       stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = "point",
                    aes(x = treat, y = rand, group = MALE, color = MALE),
                    width = 1.5) +

       stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = "line",

                    aes(x = treat, y = rand, group = MALE, color = MALE),
                    size = 1)

# Pull out the data used to create the ggplot p and select only
# those observations associated with x = 2 because that is the
# reference point for positioning the labels.

u <- ggplot_build(p)
v <- subset(u$data[[1]], x == 2)
v
str(v)

# Two vectors to tweak the x and y-positions of the text labels.
# I did this to separate the three labels at the bottom, which
# would overlap without the adjustment. I did it this way to
# make it easier for you to adjust them yourself if you wished,
# or not use them at all. On a data set with many more groups,
# this may not be a good approach - see the directlabels package
# for a probably better alternative.

adjx <- c(0, -0.05, rep(0, 7))
adjy <- c(-0.2, 0, 0.2, rep(0, 6))

# Add the text labels to the graphic and then adjust the x-axis
# labels and the x-extent of the graph.

p + geom_text(data = v, aes(x = 2.1 + adjx, y = y + adjy,
                            label = LETTERS[group])) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2), labels = c("A", "B")) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 2.5))

There's a more elegant way of doing this using the gtables package, but this is a Q & D method. Another point is that with text labels for each MALE, the legend is basically superfluous, so to remove it, add

   scale_x_discrete(guide = "none")

Dennis

Max
